Within this framework, however, the defendant was permitted to present himself on the market 
on behalf of the plaintiff or using elements of the plaintiff’s name for the purpose of informing 
third parties, even if he was no longer an officer of the plaintiff. The form and content of the 
letter to the experts were not objectionable to the extent that they corresponded to the letter to the 
client dated December 11, 2020. The content of the client letter could not have been false or in 
breach of contract, since representatives of the plaintiff had also co-signed it. 
The plaintiff takes issue with the fact that the defendant referred in the expert letter to the 
“retroactive takeover of Construction21’s operational business,” whereas the client letter referred 
to the “retroactive takeover of the candidate placement processes of Construction21.” However, 
the former statement is not incorrect. The plaintiff did not allege a single operational activity that 
it had carried out or intended to carry out with Construction21 at the time of the expert letter. 
Whether it subsequently resumed such activities is irrelevant. Furthermore, the court of first 
instance merely—and correctly—compared the business areas, processes, and infrastructure 
mentioned in the client letter or other parts of the record, which had indisputably been transferred 
to Arkadium. From this, it rightly concluded that this described “virtually the same thing” as the 
“takeover of the operational business.” The plaintiff did not address this in the appeal, so it need 
not be considered in this regard. Even insofar as the title does not mention “operational 
business,” it is not objectionable. The address on the expert’s letter is likewise unproblematic. 
4.2.3. On the other hand, it would not have been necessary for the experts’ notice to mention the 
transfer of the operational business. It would have been sufficient to state that, due to 
organizational changes, candidates (experts) currently in (ongoing) placement processes would 
have to contact Arkadium as of October 1, 2020. Consequently, there was no need to change the 
title used in the client letter (“Retroactive Takeover of Candidate Placement Processes from 
Construction21”) or to refer to a takeover of the operational business. This applies regardless of 
whether this statement was entirely or “nearly” correct. The defendant did not explain why he 
amended the client letter on these points or what necessity there was to do so. It stands to reason 
that he—or Arkadium—wished to distinguish himself or Arkadium from the plaintiff or 
Construction21. 
In any case, it is clear that the defendant violated the non-competition clause by stating in two 
places in the expert letter that Arkadium had taken over the operational business of
